title: How We Plan the Quarter
leaves: A plan the team believes it can keep, and the habit of making one.
run: Day 1 of the planning week, before the first session.

slides.html:
How we plan the quarter

Work types, sizing, commitments, and trust. A reference for our quarterly planning week.
slides.notes: Based on the How We Work deck from the DMV team's first quarterly planning, updated to the current system: three work types plus organization business, sizes in sprints, and the planning week moves (cut-off line, vote of confidence).

slides.html:
Why we are here this week

What this week produces

A realistic quarterly plan that teams believe in and can execute.

What it is not

A debate about whether we picked the right priorities.

Ground rules

  • Feedback on whether these are the right items is welcome, but it only applies to future quarterly plans.
  • This quarter's list is the best prioritization based on what we know right now.
  • This week we scope, size, and commit.

If this is our first time

  • Some prep that normally happens before planning is not done yet.
  • Expect a messier first pass.
  • The goal is a plan and a repeatable habit, not a perfect plan.
slides.notes: Say the ground rules out loud at the start. From the Quarter Zero playbook. Drop the right column after the first quarter.

slides.html:
The week at a glance

Four half-day sessions, with gaps between them to research, think, and resolve dependencies.

 

Session

What happens

Output

1

Strategy and candidates

Leads: Product manager

Goal progress, last quarter's commitments, candidates in one ranked list. Questions only.

Shared context, sizing assignments

2

Sizing

Leads: Scrum master

Size the pieces, then the Deliverables. Wide disagreement gets a second round.

Sized items, dependencies, confidence

3

Technical maintenance and capacity

Leads: Technical architect, scrum master

List the maintenance work. Count the days. Draw the cut-off line. Map slices to sprints.

What fits, and what doesn't

4

Commitment

Leads: Product manager

Vote of confidence. Each person commits out loud. Agree the stakeholder message.

Committed plan, stakeholder message
slides.notes: Before the week: the product manager shares candidate Solutions and the slice wanted this quarter; the product owner and developers break each slice into pieces small enough to size. Commitments lock on the first day of the quarter.

slides.html:
Three work types, plus organization business

Strategic

Work that advances our roadmap goals and creates new value for users. Discovery and delivery.

Default 50%

Technical maintenance

Work that keeps current services running, healthy and secure, and improves our team's ability to deliver value.

Default 25%

Small requests

Work requested by people outside our team, sent to the small request board by triage.

Default 25%

Organization business

Department meetings, organizational meetings, trainings, and administrative tasks. Not a work type.

Off the top

Every piece of work belongs to one type. Organization business comes off the top before we count the days we have for hands-on work.
slides.notes: Changes from earlier versions: "Operational" is now Technical maintenance. "Additional" is now organization business, and it is no longer a bucket we plan into; we subtract it first.

slides.html:
Examples by type

Strategic

  • New features for roadmap goals
  • Validating roadmap assumptions
  • UX solutions for roadmap services
  • Content frameworks for new services

Technical maintenance

  • Security updates and maintenance
  • Bug fixes
  • Tool migrations for cost
  • Continuous discovery setup
  • Design system upkeep
  • Analytics and measurement setup

Small requests

  • Quick usability reviews
  • Accessibility updates
  • CMS fixes and editor support
  • Data requests from leadership

Organization business

  • Department all-hands
  • Mandatory training
  • Timesheets and admin
  • Affinity groups
slides.notes: One change from earlier versions: bug fixes moved from Small requests to Technical maintenance. Bugs skip triage and go straight to the technical architect, whoever reported them.

slides.html:
Which type is it?

Ask in order. Stop at the first yes.

1

Does it advance a roadmap goal?

Strategic

2

Does it keep services running, healthy and secure, or help our team work better?

Technical maintenance

3

Did someone outside our team ask for it, and triage sent it to the small request board?

Small requests

4

Is it department or organization business, outside our service delivery?

Off the top

When maintenance work directly enables a roadmap item, pick one type for it and move on.
slides.notes: The tree is the tie-breaker. Most work is obvious; this is for the arguments.

slides.html:
Meetings and training

Technical maintenance

  • Sprint planning and retrospectives
  • Standups and team coordination
  • Quarterly planning
  • Design reviews and technical discussions
  • Process improvement meetings
  • Training the team chooses (like agile)

Organization business

  • Department all-hands
  • Organization-wide meetings
  • Required cross-department meetings
  • Mandatory HR training
  • Budget meetings where we only participate

Quick test: Is it about how our team works together or delivers services? Technical maintenance. Is it department or organization business? Off the top. For training, who decided?
slides.notes: Earlier versions used Operational and Additional. Same lists, new names.

slides.html:
How we split our time

The split is set each quarter. Start from 50/25/25 and adjust to the work at hand.

Strategic 50%

Technical maintenance 25%

Small requests 25%

Adjust for the quarter

A fixed launch date may call for more Strategic. A system near end of life may call for more Technical maintenance. Write the split and the reason down.

Some teams differ for longer

A team mostly doing discovery might run 70/15/15. A team that mostly runs existing services might run 20/50/30.

Watch for patterns

If a team keeps overriding the default the same way, that is a signal. Change its default and say why.

Equal importance doesn't mean equal time. Each type gets protected time, so none of them quietly eats the others.
slides.notes: Example: the DMV team ran 60/20/20 in Q1 because of a fixed Q2 launch, and wrote that reason in the planning overview. Rule of thumb from experience: don't skip the maintenance session. One early planning gave it an hour, and the foundation slipped.

slides.html:
Capacity math

Work it out per person, before anything gets cut.

1

Start with the quarter

13 weeks: 65 weekdays, six two-week sprints plus a spare week.

2

Take off time away

Holidays, planned vacation, and big events the team must support.

3

Take off organization business

All-hands meetings, mandatory training, timesheets.

4

Split what is left

By this quarter's work types. Strategic days divided by 10 gives Strategic sprints.

At 50% Strategic, each person has about 3 Strategic sprints in a quarter (about 3.5 at 60%). That number is what the fit check uses.

A plan built on 65 days the team doesn't have is a promise already broken.
slides.notes: The scrum master runs the math in session 3. Do it before the cut-off line, not after.

slides.html:
Size the effort, not the calendar

ELAPSED TIME

How much time will elapse between us starting and us finishing?

vs

ACTIVE TIME

How much active time will I actually spend working on this?

Elapsed time

Active time

waiting

Active time

waiting

Active time

The T-shirt size is the lavender blocks. Waiting, approvals, and scheduling go on the calendar as dates and dependencies.
slides.notes: A T-shirt size answers one question: how much focused work does this take for the people who will do it, counted in two-week sprints.

slides.html:
Two examples

Active time: what we size

Elapsed time: what we don't

Getting staff feedback

Send the email

5 min

Gap before the session

2 weeks

Hold the session

1 hr

T-shirt size: 1 hr 5 min, not 2 weeks

Google Translate API integration

Write the API integration

4 hrs

Test and debug

2 hrs

Google's API responds

200 ms

T-shirt size: about 6 hours
slides.notes: Both are XS. The two weeks in the first example still matter; they go on the calendar, not in the size.

slides.html:
What counts toward the size

Counts: active time

  • Hands-on building, design, research
  • Problem-solving and debugging
  • Testing and quality assurance
  • Documentation and deployment
  • Direct work with teammates

Doesn't count: elapsed time

  • Approvals and sign-offs
  • Scheduling delays
  • Waiting on vendors or other teams
  • Status meetings and reporting
  • Interruptions and context switching

Sizing asks how hard it is to build. Capacity planning asks how much building time we have. Waiting belongs on the calendar.
slides.notes: When someone says "this needs a lot of coordination," ask how the coordination changes the work, then put the waiting on the calendar.

slides.html:
T-shirt sizes, in sprints of focused work

XS

A few hours

S

One sprint or less

M

About 2 sprints

L

3-4 sprints

XL

5 sprints or more

Why an XL splits

A quarter has 6 sprints, and each person has about 3 for Strategic work. An XL can't finish inside one quarter, so it's a Solution, not a Deliverable. Slice it. An L fits, but only just, so check its dependencies hardest.

Why sprints

Stakeholders can read sprints, so T-shirt sizes go on the roadmap. Story points are optional inside the team, for stories, not for roadmap items.
slides.notes: This replaces the playbook's weeks-based scale (XS 1-2 weeks and so on). Calibrate against our own past work after each quarter. An XL Deliverable is a question, not a size.

1

Candidate 1

M

2

S

Running total: 3

3

Cut-off line: capacity is 8 Strategic sprints

4

Candidate 4

M

Running total: 8.5

5

Candidate 5

S

Running total: 9.5

The rule

Everything below the line is out of this quarter. The product manager can swap items across the line, but can't move the line.

The fit check

For each person or pair, add up the sizes they own and compare with their Strategic sprints. Anyone over budget means something gets cut.

Saying out loud what didn't make it is what makes the rest believable.
slides.notes: DMV example: five ranked candidates; the line fell after the Staff Training Program. Renewal reminders by text (S) fell below it and went back to the idea log for Q2. Then map each Deliverable's pieces across the six sprints to catch ordering problems the totals hide. The numbers on this slide are illustrative.

slides.html:
Vote of confidence

Before anyone commits, everyone shows a score from 1 to 5 at the same moment.

1

2

3

4

5

Anyone at 1 or 2 says why

Same moment, so nobody anchors on the loudest voice.

Fix the plan, not the person

Cut scope or change the plan until everyone is at 3 or above.

Then commit out loud

Each person says they commit to the plan.

A low vote is information, not dissent. Quiet members often have the best risk insight.
slides.notes: DMV example: two developers voted 2 on User Interface because of the legal approval. The team kept it in, named the approval date as a dependency, and agreed the product manager would escalate if it slipped. The revote was all 3 or above.

slides.html:
Making a commitment

At the end of this week, you'll verbally commit to the plan.

A commitment is a promise to try, not a guarantee.

What it means

With focus, you believe you can do your part, without working extra hours.

What it doesn't mean

You won't be in trouble. Try your best within your time and flag risks early.

What we expect

Some misses are assumed. The system is meant to push us in positive ways.

Commitments lock on the first day of the quarter. Status is updated each sprint review: Committed, On track, Off track, or Done.
slides.notes: Teams new to planning don't know how to commit yet. The first quarter can fail. Doing it anyway builds the habit, and the next one won't be so bad.

slides.html:
The trust this asks for

We're asking you to trust that...

this system will work, even if it takes time

the product manager is making the right strategic calls

working this way gets our community more value

sizing honestly means no sandbagging, from anyone

you won't get in trouble, and failure is celebrated

we all assume positive intent with one another

Trust is earned, and it can also be asked for. Today, we're asking.
slides.notes: Say this slide plainly. It is the human part of the deck: we know we are asking for something before we have earned all of it.

slides.html:
Productive tension

Be ambitious with goals

↔

Be realistic about capacity

Plan with a roadmap

↔

Adapt when plans change

Commit to the work

↔

Say early when you can't deliver

Focus on user outcomes

↔

Navigate stakeholder needs

Be accountable for outcomes

↔

Experiment, and let some fail

These tensions are intentional. The framework gives us structure; the work happens in the messy middle, and trust is what lets us live there together.
slides.notes: Nothing here resolves. That is the point.

slides.html:
This is a lot

Huge cognitive overload

If you remember 10% or understand 10%, that's pretty good!

Repetition and practice are how we get to 100%.
